title: Morning Edition
notes: Morning Edition for Tuesday, Nov 24, 2026. Covers news since the Nov 23 morning edition.

Leading this morning: Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang after President Trump’s intervention, the Pentagon’s public criticism of Canada’s military readiness, Hong Kong’s new Tai Po fire grants and its decision not to hold an official memorial, China’s planned Shenzhou-24 launch with the first foreign astronaut for its space station, and a brief air-raid alert on South Korea’s Ulleung Island. Also: an appeals ruling clearing the Iowa detonation, Rep. Jimmy Gomez’s resignation, New York’s Citi Bike e-bike fare cap, the 2031 and 2035 Women’s World Cup hosts, land-seizure powers for the Alto rail line, manslaughter charges against three Calgary officers, a 1968 London, Ont., murder solved by DNA, Brianne Jenner’s Hamilton Havoc captaincy, a bid-rigging crackdown and building reforms in Hong Kong, October visitor numbers, a new Hospital Authority chair, a costs order against activist Eddie Tse, EU caps on Chinese hybrids, Huawei’s HarmonyOS milestone, a pollution lawsuit against a Chinese-owned mine in Congo, Australia’s online safety bill, Sheikh Hasina’s planned return, Mexico’s decision to try “El Chapo Isidro” at home and the death of Molly Meldrum.

Updates on earlier stories: Nvidia (reported SEC inquiry, Nov 23 edition; Huang now reinstated); the Iowa lead azide detonation (Nov 23; appeals court now clears it); the Tai Po fire anniversary (Nov 21 and Nov 23; new grants, no official memorial).

Planned or scheduled, not confirmed when this edition was prepared: the Shenzhou-24 launch (8:18 a.m. Beijing time Nov 25, 7:18 p.m. ET Nov 24), the Iowa detonation (Wednesday morning, Nov 25), Jensen Huang’s Senate banking committee appearance (Dec 3), Jimmy Gomez’s resignation (effective Dec 1), the EU hybrid quotas (from Dec 1), Chan Kin-por’s term (from Dec 1), the Citi Bike cap (from Jan 19, 2027), Hasina’s stated Dec 16 return, the Tai Po fire anniversary (Nov 26), and passage of Australia’s online safety bill (expected this week). The Alto expropriation changes are a draft, not a tabled bill.

Photos appear on the lead and on 20 of 23 other stories. All are file photos of the people or places involved, not of this week’s events. Text-only where no suitable openly licensed photo was found: the Iowa detonation, the Hospital Authority appointment, the Congo mining lawsuit.

Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 5, China 4, World 5. China has four stories; the Chinese spy death sentence was covered in the Nov 23 edition and other candidates were mostly official or state-media items, so the section was not padded. Hong Kong has no culture story this morning. Several stories rest on a single outlet, and several Hong Kong stories rest on RTHK relaying government statements; this is noted under each story’s sources.
provenance: Compiled from the linked reporting, official releases and documents listed under each story; labels show whether a point is reported, an official statement, a claim, an allegation or analysis.

Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:19 AM and 6:25 AM ET on Nov 24; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched. Photo licences were read from each Wikimedia Commons file page’s metadata in the same session.

RTHK is Hong Kong’s government-funded broadcaster and sometimes carries Xinhua (Chinese state media) copy; CNA is Singapore’s Mediacorp news service. Wire copy carried by another outlet is marked with the agency’s name (AFP, Reuters).

Access limits: the EU’s EUR-Lex page for the hybrid regulation returned no readable content to the automated fetch, so Reuters (via Euronext) and the Guardian are cited; the South China Morning Post was not used because it blocks automated fetches; the New York Times report on Alice Huang (cited by the Guardian) is paywalled and was not opened. These are access limits, not evidence of errors.

Figures differ between sources on Nvidia’s share rise (33% at the open per CBC, about 31% at the close per the BBC), Citi Bike’s revenue-share threshold (the Guardian’s “$5.25bn” versus $5.25 million from the mayor’s office), Ulleung Island’s population (8,700 vs 9,000) and Hong Kong’s bid-rigging totals; each is noted where relevant.

stories.headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after Trump says he “convinced” the board, and Congress lines up questions
stories.deck: Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang his job back on Monday, Nov. 23, less than two weeks after he resigned over an affair with a woman some U.S. intelligence officials allege was a Chinese spy. President Trump says he persuaded the board.
stories.summary: Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang his job back on Monday, Nov. 23, less than two weeks after he resigned over an affair with a woman some U.S. intelligence officials allege was a Chinese spy. President Trump says he persuaded the board. Huang, the chipmaker’s co-founder, stepped down on Nov. 12 after admitting the relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), a businesswoman tied to the Singapore-based data-centre firm Megaspeed; China calls the spying accusations groundless. Only last week the board had said it did not plan to bring him back. On Monday chairman Harvey Jones said the reinstatement was in the “best interests” of shareholders, staff and partners, and the board said input from senior U.S. officials left it confident Huang posed no national-security risk. Trump told CNBC: “I spoke to them… And I convinced them.” He said Attorney General Todd Blanche had confirmed the government has no evidence Huang broke the law. Nvidia shares jumped about 31%, adding close to $1 trillion in market value and lifting the Nasdaq 6.5%, though the stock was still about 21% below its level a month ago, the BBC reported. Also on Monday, the Commerce Department said it plans to put Megaspeed on its trade blacklist. Huang is scheduled to face the Senate banking committee on Dec. 3 and to give transcribed interviews to several House committees. Democratic senator Chris Van Hollen called the reinstatement “exhibit A” of “political corruption”, and lawmakers from both parties are expected to press Huang on his China ties.
stories.why: This is about more than one CEO. A president personally steering who runs America’s most valuable chip company, while vouching for that person on national security, mixes politics, markets and intelligence in an unusual way. Nvidia’s chips power the AI boom, so its leadership moves retirement savings and the wider stock market. Next week’s congressional hearings are the first public test of what the government actually knows.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Allegation
stories.note: Updates the Nov 23 edition, which reported a (Reuters, unconfirmed by the BBC) SEC inquiry into Nvidia’s accounting. That inquiry is still reported only by outlets citing unnamed sources. The spying accusation against Alice Huang comes from intelligence reports described to journalists, not from charges; China denies it. Hearing dates are scheduled, not yet held.

stories.headline: Appeals court clears the Army to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa, now planned for Wednesday morning
stories.deck: A federal appeals court on Monday, Nov. 23, let the Army go ahead with blowing up 68 drums of degraded lead azide at a plant in Middletown, Iowa, hours after President Trump had ordered a pause.
stories.summary: A federal appeals court on Monday, Nov. 23, let the Army go ahead with blowing up 68 drums of degraded lead azide at a plant in Middletown, Iowa, hours after President Trump had ordered a pause. The 8th Circuit found there was an emergency reason and adequate safeguards, the BBC reported. Army Secretary Adam Telle then said the controlled detonation of the material, nearly 9,500 lb (about five tonnes), will take place on Wednesday morning, Nov. 25, calling it a “consensus decision”. Earlier on Monday Trump had written that he would not proceed unless the courts and Iowa’s Democratic governor-elect, Rob Sand, agreed, and that he would hold Sand responsible “for any and all death or destruction” if not. Sand, who takes office in January, asked the federal government to share more information with the public. The Environmental Protection Agency granted an emergency permit, saying the risk of the chemical exploding on its own was an imminent threat. The Army has warned that a plume of lead dust could reach up to 100 miles. Middletown, home to about 400 people, has a mayor who backs the detonation.
stories.why: This is a choice between two risks: leaving an unstable explosive in place or setting it off on purpose and managing the dust. Trump’s attempt to shift responsibility onto a governor who hasn’t taken office yet turned a safety decision into a political one. Whether Wednesday’s blast goes as planned, and what monitoring shows afterwards, will matter to towns downwind in Iowa and Illinois.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Claim
stories.note: Updates the Nov 23 edition, which reported the Army’s plan despite a lower-court pause. The detonation is scheduled, not confirmed, as of this edition. The 100-mile plume figure is the Army’s own warning as reported by the Guardian.

stories.headline: Rep. Jimmy Gomez says he will resign after a House ethics report finds “substantial evidence” of sexual misconduct
stories.deck: California Democrat Jimmy Gomez said on Monday, Nov. 23, he will leave Congress on Dec. 1, after a bipartisan House Ethics Committee report found substantial evidence he made unwelcome sexual advances toward a House staffer.
stories.summary: California Democrat Jimmy Gomez said on Monday, Nov. 23, he will leave Congress on Dec. 1, after a bipartisan House Ethics Committee report found substantial evidence he made unwelcome sexual advances toward a House staffer. The 19-page report says Gomez, who represents parts of Los Angeles, made unwanted advances on two occasions, including one in which he made sexual contact with the staffer, and that the conduct could amount to criminal sexual assault, NPR and the Guardian reported. Gomez said he cooperated but has “strong disagreements” with the report, which he says leaves out key parts of his testimony, while taking responsibility for “personal mistakes” outside his marriage. He had already lost his November re-election race to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres and was due to leave in January. Lawyers for the staffer, who is not named, said she testified at personal risk. House Democratic leaders Hakeem Jeffries, Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar called the report “serious and deeply troubling” and backed reforming House rules on harassment.
stories.why: Gomez was leaving anyway, so the resignation changes little in the House count. The bigger story is the incoming Democratic majority promising new rules to protect staff, which will be an early test of whether Congress polices its own members. The report’s findings are the committee’s conclusions, not a criminal verdict.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported + Allegation

stories.headline: New York caps Citi Bike member e-bike rides at $3.65 and freezes membership prices through 2029
stories.deck: From Jan. 19, 2027, Citi Bike members will pay no more than $3.65 for an e-bike ride of up to 45 minutes, under a deal Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced with Lyft on Monday, Nov. 23.
stories.summary: From Jan. 19, 2027, Citi Bike members will pay no more than $3.65 for an e-bike ride of up to 45 minutes, under a deal Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced with Lyft on Monday, Nov. 23. Members now pay 27 cents a minute on e-bikes, or $12.15 for a 45-minute ride, except trips into or out of Manhattan, which are capped at $5.40; the new cap replaces that one. The annual membership fee ($239) and member per-minute and overage fees are frozen immediately until May 26, 2029, when Lyft’s contract with the city ends, the mayor’s office said. Riders in the Reduced Fare Bike Share program are covered too. In return the city will make it easier to install charging at more than 130 stations from early 2027, let Lyft sell ads on station panels from Jan. 1, and change revenue sharing so Lyft pays the city only above a $5.25 million yearly threshold. Prices for non-members are not covered by the agreement, Gothamist reported. Mamdani said the cap would have saved riders about $11 million last year.
stories.why: For anyone who bikes to class or work, a long e-bike ride drops from about $12 to under $4, which makes Citi Bike a real alternative to the subway for some trips. The city pays nothing directly; it gives up ad space and revenue instead. The catch is the price freeze ends in 2029, when the contract is renegotiated.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported
stories.note: The Guardian’s report gives the revenue-share threshold as “$5.25bn”; the mayor’s office transcript and other reports say $5.25 million, which is used here.

stories.headline: FIFA confirms a U.S.-led bid will host the first 48-team Women’s World Cup in 2031, with the U.K. hosting in 2035
stories.deck: FIFA’s member federations approved, by acclamation on Monday, Nov. 23, the joint bid by the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 Women’s World Cup. A bid by England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland was confirmed for 2035.
stories.summary: FIFA’s member federations approved, by acclamation on Monday, Nov. 23, the joint bid by the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 Women’s World Cup. A bid by England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland was confirmed for 2035. Neither bid had a rival. The 2031 tournament will be the first women’s edition with 48 teams, matching the men’s format; the 2027 event in Brazil will have 32. The CONCACAF bid offers stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico, San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica. The U.K. bid proposes 19 venues, including Wembley, for 104 matches over 39 days. U.S. Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone told the online meeting it would be “the largest women’s sporting event in history”. The U.S. hosted alone in 1999 and 2003; England has never hosted a Women’s World Cup.
stories.why: It locks in a second U.S.-hosted World Cup within five years of the 2026 men’s tournament, so American stadiums and cities get another big global event. A 48-team field means more countries get a place, which can drive funding for women’s soccer at home. Host cities in the U.S. still have to be chosen from the 14 proposed.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported

stories.headline: Pentagon “fact sheet” accuses Canada of low military readiness and of putting “parochial” economic interests ahead of defence
stories.deck: A U.S. Department of War document posted on Monday, Nov. 23, says Canada is not meeting its NORAD or NATO obligations and has no funded plan to reach NATO’s 5% defence-spending target by 2035.
stories.summary: A U.S. Department of War document posted on Monday, Nov. 23, says Canada is not meeting its NORAD or NATO obligations and has no funded plan to reach NATO’s 5% defence-spending target by 2035. The fact sheet, first reported by Axios on Sunday, says only 41.9% of the Royal Canadian Air Force’s fleet is ready for operations this budget year, cites low army and navy readiness and notes that just one of Canada’s four Victoria-class submarines is seaworthy at a time. It accuses Ottawa of prioritising “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization”, which it says will “further burden… the American taxpayer”, and points to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s ongoing review of the F-35 purchase. It also says Canada is deferring the biggest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election. The document follows a Washington Post report that War Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a classified memo restricting U.S. military contact with Canada; U.S. Senator Mike Rounds called those limits largely symbolic. Defence Minister David McGuinty’s office was not immediately available for comment, CBC reported, and did not respond to the Globe and Mail late Monday.
stories.why: Washington is using public pressure to push Canada on two things at once: more defence money and finishing the F-35 deal, at a time when trade relations are already strained. The readiness numbers are the U.S. government’s figures, and Ottawa had not responded publicly when this edition was prepared. How Carney answers will shape both NORAD co-operation and the trade talks.
stories.label: Official statement + Claim + Reported
stories.note: The fact sheet’s criticisms are the U.S. government’s assessments. The Pentagon document itself was not opened for this edition; its contents are described by CBC and the Globe and Mail.

stories.headline: Draft budget bill would give Ottawa sweeping land-seizure powers for the Alto high-speed rail line
stories.deck: Proposed changes in the government’s planned Budget 2026 implementation bill would let Ottawa expropriate land for the Toronto–Quebec City Alto line without public hearings and hand it directly to a private consortium, CBC News reported on Tuesday, Nov. 24.
stories.summary: Proposed changes in the government’s planned Budget 2026 implementation bill would let Ottawa expropriate land for the Toronto–Quebec City Alto line without public hearings and hand it directly to a private consortium, CBC News reported on Tuesday, Nov. 24. The draft would exempt Alto from the whole Expropriation Act and from parts of the Railway Safety Act, the Impact Assessment Act and railway crossing rules. Crossing disputes for farms and roads split by the line would go to private arbitration, with costs shared up to $25,000 per party. The government could also block new work on a targeted property for four years and hold a right of first refusal for up to eight years before deciding whether to take it, said land-use lawyer Ajay Gajaria, who called it potentially “the largest expropriation project in modern Canadian history”. Alto declined to comment. The Conservatives and Bloc Québécois oppose the project; NDP Leader Avi Lewis supports high-speed rail but has reservations about the powers. The federal government calls Alto a “bold step” for Canada’s transport needs.
stories.why: High-speed rail between Canada’s biggest cities needs a straight, fenced corridor, which means taking land, and these rules decide how much say owners get. Removing public hearings speeds construction but shifts power away from farmers and towns along the route. It is a draft, so the fight in Parliament over these clauses is still ahead.
stories.label: Official proposal + Reported + Analysis
stories.note: Based on one outlet’s reading of draft legislation; the bill has not been tabled or passed. Gajaria’s views are expert analysis.

stories.headline: Three Calgary police officers charged with manslaughter in the 2024 death of Jon Wells, an unarmed Blood Tribe man
stories.deck: Alberta’s police watchdog on Monday, Nov. 23, charged three Calgary Police Service constables with manslaughter and assault causing bodily harm over the death of Jon Wells, 42, who died after being restrained in a hotel lobby in September 2024.
stories.summary: Alberta’s police watchdog on Monday, Nov. 23, charged three Calgary Police Service constables with manslaughter and assault causing bodily harm over the death of Jon Wells, 42, who died after being restrained in a hotel lobby in September 2024. The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) said its two-year investigation found reasonable grounds to believe offences were committed; Constables Roy Braun, Filip Poskovic and Vincent Washington were released on undertakings and the case returns to court on Jan. 6, 2027. ASIRT had said in 2024, based on body-camera video, that Wells was unarmed, said “I don’t want to die” and was tackled, punched, hit with stun guns and left face down in handcuffs, leg restraints and a spit hood before he was found unresponsive. Lawyers for all three officers said their clients deny the charges and will defend themselves. Wells’s sister Leslie said he “deserved to be protected, treated with compassion”.
stories.why: Charging officers with manslaughter is a serious step for a police watchdog, and the case adds to long-running concern about how police treat First Nations people. The officers are presumed innocent; a court will now test the watchdog’s evidence, including body-camera footage the public has not seen.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported + Allegation

stories.headline: London, Ont., police say DNA genealogy has identified the killer of 16-year-old Jackie Dunleavy, 58 years later
stories.deck: Police in London, Ont., said on Monday, Nov. 23, that genetic genealogy has identified the man who killed Jackie Dunleavy, a 16-year-old found strangled in 1968 after a shift at a convenience store.
stories.summary: Police in London, Ont., said on Monday, Nov. 23, that genetic genealogy has identified the man who killed Jackie Dunleavy, a 16-year-old found strangled in 1968 after a shift at a convenience store. They named him as Michael Joseph Moore, who was 25 at the time and later became a London firefighter, retiring as a captain. He was never a suspect. Moore died in 2018, so no charges can be laid. Police Chief Thai Truong credited investigators past and present and the “careful preservation of evidence”. Dunleavy’s younger brother attended the announcement but did not give interviews. The force says it is working on nine cold cases.
stories.why: It shows how decades-old evidence, if stored properly, can still give families answers through DNA databases built for family-tree research. Here there will be no trial, so the police account is the final word.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported
stories.note: Moore’s identification is the police conclusion; he cannot be tried. Single outlet.

stories.headline: Hong Kong announces HK$630 million in new Tai Po fire grants but says it will hold no official memorial for the anniversary
stories.deck: Ahead of the first anniversary of the Wang Fuk Court fire on Nov. 26, the Hong Kong government said on Tuesday, Nov. 24 (Hong Kong time), that it will not host official memorial events, and announced two new grants for victims worth about HK$630 million.
stories.summary: Ahead of the first anniversary of the Wang Fuk Court fire on Nov. 26, the Hong Kong government said on Tuesday, Nov. 24 (Hong Kong time), that it will not host official memorial events, and announced two new grants for victims worth about HK$630 million. Chief Secretary Eric Chan told Commercial Radio that many community and religious memorials are already planned, that the government would not obstruct lawful ones and might help with transport, but urged people to choose “carefully” because some online were trying to use memorials to “make trouble”, Hong Kong Free Press reported. Under the new “New Beginning” grants, each flat owner gets HK$300,000 in two instalments (end of December 2026 and end of June 2027), and the family of each person who died gets HK$200,000 in December, paid through social workers without applications. Families of foreign domestic helpers who died will be contacted through consulates. Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak said the HK$4.5 billion support fund is now largely used up. The fire spread across seven blocks of the estate in Tai Po during renovation work in November 2025, killing 168 people.
stories.why: The money matters for families still rebuilding a year on, and paying owners even if they sold their flats to the government is a practical choice. But declining to hold an official memorial, while warning about people who “make trouble”, signals how carefully authorities are managing public grief, after a book launch with migrant survivors was abruptly called off (Nov 23 edition).

The “safeguard” quotas, announced in the EU’s Official Journal, apply for up to 200 days while an investigation into hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports continues; over that period China’s share works out to about 191,000 cars, the Guardian reported. Under trade rules the caps must cover all big exporters, so Japan, Turkey, South Korea, the U.K. and others also get quotas, but most are set high enough to cover their current shipments, Reuters reported. The EU says China’s hybrid exports worldwide jumped from 191,000 in 2023 to 1.124 million in 2025, as Chinese makers shifted to hybrids after the EU put tariffs on fully electric cars in 2024. The measure follows an October agreement between Brussels and Beijing. China’s commerce ministry said it hoped the EU would abide by that consensus and reserved its rights.
stories.why: Chinese carmakers found a way around EU tariffs on electric cars by shipping hybrids, and Europe is now closing that gap to protect its own car industry and jobs. It is a sign that trade friction between China and its big export markets is shifting from tariffs to quotas. Any permanent measure would need broad support from EU countries.

stories.headline: South Korea sounds a brief air-raid alert on Ulleung Island as Russian military planes approach its airspace

stories.headline: Australia’s online safety bill, set to pass with Greens support, would let people sue platforms and fine them up to 5% of global revenue
stories.deck: Australia’s Labor government struck a deal with the Greens on Tuesday, Nov. 24, to pass a “digital duty of care” law that would expose social media and tech firms to fines of up to 5% of their worldwide revenue and give individuals a right to sue.
stories.summary: Australia’s Labor government struck a deal with the Greens on Tuesday, Nov. 24, to pass a “digital duty of care” law that would expose social media and tech firms to fines of up to 5% of their worldwide revenue and give individuals a right to sue. The bill would replace a patchwork of industry codes with one legal duty on social media, games, apps, search and AI chatbots to provide a safe online environment, targeting harms such as child sexual abuse material, fake nude images, self-harm promotion and terrorism. From late 2027 Australians aged 16 and over would be able to switch off algorithm-driven feeds, and “endless scroll” features may be curbed. The maximum fine had previously been proposed at A$109 million, Al Jazeera reported. Communications Minister Anika Wells said she had met the U.S. ambassador about the laws and dared firms to challenge them: “bring it on.” The opposition Coalition opposed the bill, citing free-speech concerns. The government expects it to pass parliament this week.
stories.why: Australia already banned social media for under-16s; this goes further by making platforms legally responsible for harm to everyone and letting users take them to court. Other governments watch Australia’s tech laws closely, and the minister’s meeting with the U.S. ambassador shows Washington is paying attention too.

stories.headline: Mexico says it will put alleged cartel leader “El Chapo Isidro” on trial at home despite a U.S. extradition request
stories.deck: Mexico’s attorney general said on Monday, Nov. 23, that Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, will be tried in Mexico, even though the United States has asked for his extradition.
stories.summary: Mexico’s attorney general said on Monday, Nov. 23, that Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, will be tried in Mexico, even though the United States has asked for his extradition. Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was captured after an hours-long firefight at a compound in Guasave, Sinaloa, on Friday night, Nov. 20, in which four Mexican soldiers and 16 alleged gunmen were killed, according to Mexico’s defence ministry. He faces Mexican charges of weapons offences and methamphetamine possession with intent to sell; in the U.S. he faces six charges including narcoterrorism and running a continuing criminal enterprise. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Washington had requested extradition. President Claudia Sheinbaum said U.S. authorities gave intelligence support but did not take part on the ground, and U.S. surveillance drones were authorised to help track him.
stories.why: Keeping a top U.S. target for a Mexican trial is a statement of sovereignty at a time of pressure from Washington over cartels, even as the two countries co-operated on intelligence for the raid. It could strain relations, and the extradition request remains on the table.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported + Allegation
stories.note: The charges are allegations. The death toll is from Mexico’s defence ministry as reported by Al Jazeera.

stories.headline: Molly Meldrum, the Countdown host who shaped decades of Australian pop, dies at 83
stories.deck: Ian “Molly” Meldrum, the broadcaster and music journalist who hosted the ABC’s Countdown and championed acts from INXS to Kylie Minogue, died peacefully in a Melbourne hospital on Monday, Nov. 23, local time, his family said. He was 83.
stories.summary: Ian “Molly” Meldrum, the broadcaster and music journalist who hosted the ABC’s Countdown and championed acts from INXS to Kylie Minogue, died peacefully in a Melbourne hospital on Monday, Nov. 23, local time, his family said. He was 83. On Countdown, which ran from 1974 to 1987, an endorsement from Meldrum (“do yourself a favour”) could make a record a hit, and his chaotic, Stetson-hatted interviews with stars became famous, including a nervous 1977 sit-down with the then Prince Charles. Earlier, while in London, he landed a scoop from John Lennon that the Beatles were splitting up, ABC News reported. In 2014 he became the first non-recording artist inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame. He had lived with a brain injury since a fall in 2011. King Charles called him “a true giant of the music industry”, Elton John also paid tribute, and Victoria’s premier said a state funeral will be held.
stories.why: Before streaming and algorithms, a single TV host could decide what a whole country listened to, and Meldrum was the clearest example. His push for local acts helped Australian musicians reach the world, a reminder of how much one passionate champion can matter to an industry.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement
stories.note: Meldrum died on Nov. 23 Melbourne time (Nov. 22 in New York), before the Nov 23 edition was prepared, but it was not covered there.
